rnn.definition: An RNN processes a sequence in order, one token at a time.

hidden_state.definition: At every position, the hidden state contains the information the network has chosen to carry forward from the prefix seen so far.

initial_state.definition: The model begins with an initial state, often a vector of zeros.

final_state.definition: The final state therefore acts as a compact representation of everything the RNN has processed.

recurrent_transition.definition: Information needed at the end must pass through every intermediate recurrent transition, and each transition can weaken or overwrite it.

bottleneck.definition: The bottleneck therefore defines a requirement for the next architecture.

the customer cannot access the account.current_state: The example is used to show that the final state must preserve the subject established by "customer," the failure expressed by "cannot access," the relevant relationships, and the latest token "account." The section concludes that these earlier details may be weakened, overwritten, or become indistinguishable through repeated updates, motivating direct access to earlier representations.

sec_01_01.abstract: This section taught that an RNN processes tokens sequentially by repeatedly updating a fixed-size hidden state. The state compresses the prefix seen so far, allowing downstream predictions, but every new token must be mixed into the same representation. As sequences lengthen, earlier details can be weakened, overwritten, or become indistinguishable, creating failures on long-range dependencies. The section therefore established the need for an architecture that lets a position access relevant earlier representations directly rather than relying exclusively on one recurrent summary.

sec_01_01.title: Sequence Compression into a Recurrent State

chapter_rollups.ch01: This chapter built an understanding of how recurrent neural networks process sequences through repeated updates to a fixed-size hidden state. It showed that this state compresses the preceding prefix, requiring each new token to overwrite or merge information into the same representation. By the end, the reader can explain why long sequences weaken or obscure earlier details, identify the resulting long-range dependency problem, and motivate architectures that directly access relevant earlier representations.
